analysis.one_liner: Doubles the number of drugs Medicare must negotiate prices for and tightens the price caps.
analysis.headline: The bill to expand Medicare's drug price negotiation program never got a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The SMART Prices Act would build on the 2022 law that lets Medicare negotiate prices for the most expensive brand-name drugs. It would roughly double the number of drugs Medicare negotiates each year, cut from 7 to 11 years down to 3 years the wait before a drug becomes eligible for negotiation, lower the maximum prices Medicare can pay, and repeal a rule that stops Medicare from getting involved in drug pricing negotiations. The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2023 and no further action was ever taken on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers. Millions of people on Medicare would pay less out of pocket for widely used brand-name drugs as negotiated prices arrived years sooner and covered more drugs, and the federal government would spend less on prescription drugs under Parts B and D.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare to negotiate prices for 20 drugs starting in 2026 and 40 drugs per year starting in 2027, up from 10 in 2026 and 15-20 in later years under current law [S2] [S3].
Cuts the time a drug must be on the market before Medicare can negotiate its price from 7 years for small-molecule drugs and 11 years for biologics down to 3 years for both [S2] [S3].
Lowers the ceiling on the maximum price Medicare can be charged: to 55% of list price for drugs with extended monopoly, and 30% for long-monopoly drugs, down from 65% and 40% [S3].
Repeals the 'noninterference clause,' a rule that bars Medicare from intervening in price negotiations between drug manufacturers, pharmacies, and plan sponsors [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would see Medicare-negotiated prices arrive years earlier, apply to far more drugs, and fall closer to a ceiling that is well below list price.

drawbacks.text: Tighter negotiated prices and shorter monopoly protection could reduce expected returns on new drugs, which the pharmaceutical industry argues would lead companies to launch fewer medicines, especially ones for small patient populations [S2].

Expanding negotiation to 40 drugs a year and shortening the waiting period to 3 years means prices could be set on drugs early in their life cycle, before their real-world value and safety record are well established.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries and federal taxpayers the gains are direct and large: lower prices on far more drugs, years sooner, with no change in access rules for patients. The main cost is a possible slowdown in new drug development over time, a tradeoff the bill's supporters accepted in exchange for immediate savings; the bill does nothing about high drug prices for people with private insurance or no insurance.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2023 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar and 24 original cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, introduced the bill on April 25, 2023 [S3] [S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
The Finance Committee took no further action; no markup, hearing on the bill, or floor vote appears in the bill's action history [S5] [S1].
The bill accumulated 29 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill receiving a vote [S4] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: they keep the slower negotiation timetable and higher price ceilings of the 2022 law, and Medicare beneficiaries continue paying the resulting prices. The senators who supported the bill gained nothing from its death.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SMART Prices Act and recruited 24 original cosponsors, all Democrats or independents.

for.name: 29 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; the bill never attracted a single Republican cosponsor and never reached a vote.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Brand-name drug makers and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed expansion of Medicare drug price negotiation and argued it would reduce investment in new medicines; no member of the Senate majority championed the bill's floor consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and with a Democratic-led Senate the bill still never left committee.

industries.note: Medicare would negotiate prices for twice as many drugs starting years earlier, with lower price ceilings, cutting revenue from the government's largest drug buyer. The industry's gain from the bill's death is higher prices paid by Medicare and its beneficiaries.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D plan sponsors
industries.note: Repealing the noninterference clause would let Medicare intervene in negotiations between manufacturers, pharmacies, and plans, changing the leverage PBMs and plans have long held in the supply chain [S2] [S3]. Lower negotiated drug prices could also reduce plan costs and premiums.
The bill cuts the pre-negotiation waiting period for biologics from 11 years to 3 years, exposing them to negotiated prices far earlier in their life cycle [S3].
